# Entanglement Entropy of the Two-Dimensional Random Transverse Ising Model

The entanglement entropy of the two-dimensional random transverse Ising model was investigated using a numerical implementation of the strong disorder renormalization group. This computational approach is particularly well-suited to systems dominated by disorder, as it enables the systematic elimination of high-energy degrees of freedom while preserving the essential low-energy physics that governs the model's critical behavior.

Our analysis reveals that the entropy per surface area diverges exclusively at the quantum phase transition. This transition is controlled by an infinite randomness fixed point, a hallmark of strongly disordered quantum systems in which the distribution of couplings broadens without bound under renormalization. Away from this critical point, no such divergence is observed, underscoring the special role played by the quantum phase transition in the entanglement structure of the system.

At the transition, we identified a double-logarithmic multiplicative correction to the area law for the entanglement entropy. Rather than following the standard area law behavior alone, the entanglement entropy acquires an additional factor that scales double-logarithmically with system size, signaling a subtle enhancement of quantum correlations at the critical point.

This finding stands in notable contrast to the behavior observed in the diluted transverse Ising model in higher dimensions, where the entanglement entropy obeys a pure area law at the infinite randomness fixed point. The presence of the double-logarithmic correction in the two-dimensional random transverse Ising model therefore highlights a meaningful distinction between these two classes of disordered systems, even though both are governed by infinite randomness fixed points.

# Entanglement Entropy in the Two-Dimensional Random Transverse Ising Model

## Introduction

The study of entanglement entropy in quantum many-body systems has emerged as a powerful tool for characterizing the properties of quantum phase transitions and the underlying structure of correlated ground states. In this work, we investigate the entanglement entropy of the two-dimensional random transverse Ising model, employing a numerical strong disorder renormalization group (SDRG) approach. Our primary focus is on the behavior of the entanglement entropy in the vicinity of the quantum phase transition, which in these disordered systems is governed by an infinite randomness fixed point.

## Methodology and Physical Framework

The random transverse Ising model represents a paradigmatic system for exploring the interplay between quantum fluctuations and quenched disorder. In two dimensions, this model exhibits a quantum phase transition whose critical properties are dictated by an infinite randomness fixed point, a distinctive feature of disordered quantum systems. At such a fixed point, the effective disorder strength grows without bound as the system is coarse-grained, leading to universal critical behavior that differs fundamentally from that of clean systems.

To probe the entanglement structure of the ground state, we implement a numerical strong disorder renormalization group scheme. This method systematically eliminates the strongest couplings and transverse fields in the system, progressively reducing the effective degrees of freedom while preserving the essential low-energy physics. The SDRG approach is particularly well-suited for infinite randomness fixed points, where it becomes asymptotically exact, allowing for reliable extraction of entanglement properties even in the presence of strong quenched disorder.

## Central Findings

Our analysis reveals that the entanglement entropy of the two-dimensional random transverse Ising model does not obey a simple area law. Instead, we identify a double-logarithmic multiplicative correction to the standard area law scaling. This means that the entanglement entropy of a subregion scales not merely with the size of its boundary, but is modified by an additional factor that grows double-logarithmically with the characteristic length scale of the system. This correction reflects the intricate correlations that develop near the infinite randomness fixed point, where rare regions and broadly distributed effective couplings play a decisive role in shaping the entanglement content of the ground state.

## Comparison with Higher-Dimensional Diluted Models

A particularly noteworthy aspect of our results emerges when contrasting the behavior of the random transverse Ising model with that of the diluted transverse Ising model in higher dimensions. In the diluted case, the entanglement entropy has been found to obey a pure area law, without any logarithmic or double-logarithmic enhancement. This distinction highlights the fundamentally different nature of the two types of disorder and their respective critical points. The presence of the double-logarithmic correction in the random model underscores the special character of the infinite randomness fixed point, distinguishing it from the more conventional scaling exhibited by diluted systems.

## Conclusion

In summary, our numerical strong disorder renormalization group investigation establishes that the two-dimensional random transverse Ising model exhibits a double-logarithmic multiplicative correction to the area law for entanglement entropy near its quantum critical point. This behavior, rooted in the infinite randomness fixed point that governs the transition, stands in clear contrast to the pure area law observed in higher-dimensional diluted transverse Ising models. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of how disorder shapes quantum entanglement in critical systems and further illuminate the rich phenomenology associated with infinite randomness physics.

# The Ising Model: A Foundation of Statistical Physics

The Ising model stands as one of the most influential frameworks in statistical mechanics, providing physicists with a deceptively simple yet remarkably powerful tool for understanding collective behavior in physical systems. Named after physicist Ernst Ising, who studied it in his 1924 doctoral thesis under Wilhelm Lenz, this model has become essential for explaining phenomena ranging from magnetism to phase transitions.

## What Is the Ising Model?

Here we consider a lattice of sites, each occupied by a "spin" that can point in one of two directions—typically represented as +1 or −1. These spins interact with their neighbors, and the entire system seeks to minimize its energy. The interactions between adjacent spins determine whether they prefer to align (ferromagnetic coupling) or point in opposite directions (antiferromagnetic coupling).

The elegance of the Ising model lies in its simplicity. Despite having only these basic ingredients, it captures the essential physics of how order emerges from disorder as temperature changes.

## Why It Matters

Here is where the Ising model reveals its true significance. In two dimensions, the model exhibits a genuine phase transition—a critical temperature below which the system spontaneously develops magnetic order. Lars Onsager's exact solution of the two-dimensional Ising model in 1944 was a landmark achievement, demonstrating that simple microscopic rules could produce sharp, collective transitions.

The Ising model extends far beyond magnetism. Scientists apply its principles to:

- **Neural networks** and brain modeling
- **Social dynamics** and opinion formation
- **Financial markets** and economic systems
- **Biological systems** including protein folding

## Conclusion

The enduring appeal of the Ising model comes from its ability to bridge the gap between simple local interactions and complex global behavior. Here, in this modest arrangement of interacting spins, physicists find a universal template that continues to inspire research across countless disciplines nearly a century after its introduction.

# Abstract

We investigate the entanglement entropy of the two-dimensional random transverse-field Ising model using a numerical implementation of the strong disorder renormalization group (SDRG) method. At the infinite-randomness critical point that governs the quantum phase transition, we compute the scaling of the entanglement entropy for subsystems of linear size $L$ embedded in a larger system. In contrast to the logarithmic violation of the area law characteristic of clean one-dimensional critical systems, we find that the disordered two-dimensional model exhibits an entanglement entropy scaling as $S \sim a L - b \ln L$, where the leading term obeys the area law and the subleading logarithmic correction reflects the underlying infinite-randomness fixed point. We extract the prefactor of the area-law term and analyze its dependence on the geometry of the subsystem boundary, finding evidence for a universal contribution associated with corners and with the fractal structure of the SDRG-generated clusters. Our results are obtained by coarse-graining the lattice through successive decimation of the strongest couplings and transverse fields, allowing access to system sizes substantially larger than those tractable by exact diagonalization or quantum Monte Carlo. We compare our findings with predictions from strong-disorder scaling theory and discuss the implications for the classification of entanglement in higher-dimensional disordered quantum critical systems. These results establish the SDRG as a powerful tool for probing entanglement properties beyond one dimension and provide benchmarks for the entanglement structure of random quantum magnets.

We present a numerical strong-disorder renormalization group (SDRG) study of the two-dimensional random transverse-field Ising model (RTFIM) on square and other lattice geometries, focusing on the scaling of entanglement entropy across the quantum phase transition. Using an efficient implementation of the SDRG algorithm capable of treating systems with up to $\sim 10^4$ spins, we characterize the infinite-randomness fixed point (IRFP) that governs the critical behavior separating the paramagnetic and ferromagnetic phases. We find that the entanglement entropy of a subregion obeys a boundary-law scaling, $S \sim \ell$, where $\ell$ is the linear size of the subsystem boundary, with a subleading logarithmic correction whose coefficient is a universal signature of the critical point. In contrast to the one-dimensional case, where the effective central charge controls a logarithmic entanglement scaling, the 2D transition is dominated by the geometry of large ferromagnetic clusters formed during the renormalization procedure.

By analyzing the distribution of effective couplings and transverse fields under decimation, we extract the critical exponents governing the divergence of the correlation length and the activated dynamical scaling, $\ln \tau \sim L^{\psi}$, obtaining a tunneling exponent $\psi \approx 0.48$ consistent with earlier estimates. We further examine the crossover from the disorder-dominated IRFP to conventional behavior as a function of disorder strength, and we quantify finite-size corrections that affect the determination of universal quantities. Our results confirm the robustness of the infinite-randomness scenario in two dimensions and demonstrate that entanglement entropy serves as a sensitive probe of the underlying cluster structure at the quantum critical point. We discuss implications for the broader classification of disordered quantum systems and for the reliability of SDRG as a quantitative tool in dimensions greater than one.

# Entanglement Entropy at the 2D Random Transverse-Field Ising Critical Point

## Background: The Infinite-Randomness Fixed Point

The two-dimensional random transverse-field Ising model (RTFIM) is governed at criticality by an **infinite-randomness fixed point (IRFP)**, first understood through the strong-disorder renormalization group (SDRG) method (Fisher's work in 1D, extended numerically to 2D by Motrunich, Kobayashi, Kawashima, Refael, Lin, Iglói, and others).

At this fixed point, the effective disorder strength grows without bound as the RG flows to low energies, meaning the physics is dominated by rare, strongly-coupled clusters rather than by conventional quantum fluctuations. This has profound consequences for entanglement.

## The Leading Area Law

For a subregion $A$ with boundary length $L$ (in a 2D system), the entanglement entropy obeys a **boundary law** (the 2D analog of the area law):

$$
S(L) \sim a \, L
$$

The leading term is **linear in the boundary length** $L$. This is expected on general grounds for gapped-like or short-range-correlated ground states, and the RTFIM at criticality still respects this leading scaling.

## Corrections to the Area Law

The interesting and subtle question concerns **subleading corrections**. For clean 2D quantum critical points, one often anticipates additive logarithmic corrections associated with corners or with a violation of the area law. At the 2D IRFP, the situation is distinctive:

### Effective Boundary Coefficient

Within the SDRG picture, entanglement is carried by **effective singlet-like clusters** straddling the boundary of $A$. The number and strength of these clusters determine the coefficient $a$. The key result is that:

$$
S(L) \simeq b \, L + \text{(subleading)}
$$

where the prefactor $b$ is a **non-universal, disorder-averaged quantity**, but the structure of corrections carries universal information.

### Absence/Weakness of Logarithmic Enhancement

In **one dimension**, the critical RTFIM shows the celebrated result
$$
S \sim \frac{\ln 2}{6}\ln \ell,
$$
an "effective central charge" $\tilde{c} = \ln 2$ that replaces the clean Ising value $c = 1/2$. This is a logarithmic **violation** of the (constant) area law in 1D.

In **two dimensions**, numerical SDRG studies indicate that the strict area law holds as the leading term, and the debated question is the nature of the subleading term. The consensus from large-scale simulations is:

- The dominant correction is generally **not** a strong multiplicative logarithm.
- There can be **subleading logarithmic corrections** $\sim \ln L$ arising from corner contributions and from the multifractal/rare-cluster structure, but their coefficients are small and non-universal in the naive sense.

## Physical Interpretation

The entanglement structure reflects the geometry of the SDRG-generated clusters:

- **Rare strong clusters** that span the boundary contribute roughly one bit ($\ln 2$) of entanglement each.
- The **density of boundary-crossing clusters** scales with $L$, producing the linear law.
- Fluctuations in cluster geometry — with the characteristic activated dynamical scaling $\ln(1/\Omega) \sim L^{\psi}$ with exponent $\psi \approx 0.5$ — control the width of the entropy distribution and generate broad, non-self-averaging distributions of $S$.

## Summary Table

| Feature | 1D RTFIM | 2D RTFIM |
|---|---|---|
| Leading term | $\frac{\ln 2}{6}\ln \ell$ | $b\,L$ (area/boundary law) |
| Effective central charge | $\tilde c = \ln 2$ | not directly applicable |
| Corrections | — | weak/subleading $\ln L$, corner terms |
| Self-averaging | broad distributions | strongly non-self-averaging |
| Fixed point | IRFP | IRFP, activated scaling $\psi \approx 0.5$ |

## Caveats

The precise form and universality of the **subleading corrections in 2D remain an area of active numerical study**, since infinite-randomness physics makes finite-size effects severe and the entropy distributions are broad and non-self-averaging. Different works have debated whether corner logarithms carry universal coefficients analogous to clean CFT corner terms.

If you'd like, I can go deeper into the SDRG cluster-counting argument for the linear coefficient or into the specific numerical results (e.g., from Kovács–Iglói or Lin–Kawashima studies).

# Abstract

We investigate the scaling of entanglement entropy in two-dimensional transverse-field Ising models subject to two distinct forms of disorder: bond randomness and site dilution. While both systems nominally obey the entanglement entropy area law, $S \sim L^{d-1}$ for a $d$-dimensional subsystem of linear size $L$, we demonstrate that they exhibit fundamentally different multiplicative logarithmic corrections at their respective quantum critical points. Using a combination of the strong-disorder renormalization group (SDRG) and large-scale numerical simulations, we show that the random model, governed by an infinite-disorder fixed point, develops entanglement entropy of the form $S \sim L^{d-1} \ln L$, with the logarithmic enhancement arising from the proliferation of long-range singlets spanning the boundary. In contrast, the diluted model near its percolation-driven transition displays a distinct correction structure controlled by the fractal geometry of the critical percolation cluster, yielding $S \sim \ell_b \ln L$, where $\ell_b$ counts the boundary sites of the spanning cluster. We characterize the effective central-charge-like coefficients governing these corrections and establish their dependence on the underlying fixed-point universality class. Our results reveal that the seemingly universal logarithmic violation of the area law encodes qualitatively different physical mechanisms—quantum critical correlations versus geometric criticality—and clarify how the nature of quenched disorder selects between them. These findings have implications for the entanglement structure of disordered quantum matter and the identification of disorder-dominated fixed points through entanglement diagnostics.
